**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. English Language 2 (0730), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2026. Paper 2: Section A - Composition; Section B - Prescribed Texts; Section C - Creative Writing. Duration: two hours fifteen minutes.**

Instructions to candidates: ANSWER ONE QUESTION FROM EACH SECTION. ALL QUESTIONS CARRY EQUAL MARKS.

Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks.

Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

A pre-prepared or memorised answer will earn you little or no marks.

**SECTION A - COMPOSITION (20 marks)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (10 marks); Expression (8 marks); Accuracy (2 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write about from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity. You should write between 500 and 550 words.

questions.enonce_markdown: **a)** Write a story that illustrates the idiom, 'Rome wasn't built in a day.'
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Open with the idiom, said by a character, and promise a story that proves it.
2. Show the impatient hero and his unrealistic dream (quick, large success).
3. Show the setback caused by hurrying (the lost savings).
4. Show the patient restart: small steps, discipline, growth over years.
5. Close by returning to the idiom, so that the story clearly illustrates it.

**Model composition (536 words)**

When my grandmother wanted to end an argument, she never raised her voice; she simply said, "Rome wasn't built in a day." As a boy in Buea, I believed it was one of those old sayings that elders use when they have no better answer. It took the collapse of my first great dream, at the age of twenty-two, to teach me that she had been answering me all along.

I had just finished my diploma in tailoring and fashion design, and my head was full of fireworks. I did not want to sew shirts for neighbours at five hundred francs a piece. I wanted a shop on Molyko Road, a signboard with my name in gold letters, and a car by the end of the year. "Slowly, Ntui," Grandma would say, shelling groundnuts on the veranda. "A tree does not grow taller because you stare at it." I laughed and told her that her generation had all the time in the world, but mine did not.

Then a classmate introduced me to a man who promised that any money I invested with him would be doubled within three weeks. I sold my sewing machine, the only property I owned, and handed him the entire amount. On the appointed day his telephone was switched off, and his office had been empty for a week. I sat on the roadside and understood, with a cold feeling in my stomach, that I had lost everything for the sake of hurrying.

For a month I hardly left my room. It was Grandma who broke the silence. One morning she came in carrying a small bundle tied in a wrapper and placed it on my bed. Inside were the savings she had kept for years from selling vegetables in the market, enough to buy a second-hand machine. "I am not giving you a fortune," she said gently. "I am giving you a beginning. Rome wasn't built in a day, my son, and neither was this market, which I joined with a single basket of tomatoes."

I accepted the money with shame and began again, this time differently. I sewed school uniforms, mended trousers and altered wedding dresses, and I smiled at every customer, however small the order. I kept a notebook in which I recorded every franc earned and spent. When I had saved enough, I bought a second machine, then a third, and I took on Etienne, a hungry apprentice with the same impatience I had once carried. When some months brought nothing, Grandma's voice returned: one brick at a time.

Eight years have passed. Today my workshop on Molyko Road employs eleven young people, and the signboard above the door carries my name, painted in plain blue because gold is not necessary for pride. Last Christmas, Grandma sat in the front row of our small fashion show, beaming at the dresses I had made for her friends from the market. I gave her the seat I had always owed her.

Whenever a new apprentice grumbles that success is too slow, I only smile and repeat the proverb, and I watch the lesson begin its long journey, just as it did in me: Rome wasn't built in a day.

**Marking grid**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 10 | A real story (characters, setting, problem, resolution) that clearly illustrates that great results need time; the idiom is used at the start and end; paragraphs in logical order, within 500 to 550 words. |
| Expression | 8 | Vivid narrative verbs, dialogue, varied sentence openings and connectors, a consistent past-tense narrative voice, Cameroonian context made concrete. |
| Accuracy | 2 | Correct tenses, agreement, spelling and punctuation, especially in dialogue. |

**Common errors**

- Writing an essay about patience instead of a story: the idiom must be shown through events, not explained in general terms.
- Telling the story in a hurry (a few lines of summary and a sudden happy ending): the story must itself take its time, with a slow, believable build-up.
